rationale: B wins by a slight margin because it finds two real routes A leaves on the floor: offline architecture and the no-pricing security feature story. A's "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" is a speculative replacement story without a named displaced incumbent, while B's "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm" turns a supplied fact into a beat-specific business angle. B is not clean - "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is over-written causality - but it gives the founder more distinct press doors to test.
gaps_in_A: Refusing "Notion ships offline-first editing" as "a bare feature description" throws away a usable architecture and enterprise-reliability angle; the update says offline editing now works with no connection and syncs on reconnect.
No angle uses "no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans"; that is a concrete SaaS pricing/procurement hook, not bookkeeping.
"Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents displacement until there is evidence the pilots are replacing anything.
The middle of the set overclusters around compliance: "Encryption keys," "Can a workspace wiki," and "Notion lets EU and Australian" are different, but not as different as the labels claim.
gaps_in_B: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" invents concession and causality; the facts only say enterprise customers can hold keys via AWS KMS.
"the bank pilots are the proof it landed with the hardest buyers" oversells pilots as adoption proof; pilots are not deployments and no bank is named.
"always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" is a good provocation but unsupported as stated; one offline launch does not prove a category reversal.
"security-upsell norm" and the "SSO tax" frame are outside the update; the set correctly asks for competitor examples, but the headline is ahead of the evidence.
